### Conductor

Conductor is proprietary software with a macOS app, managed cloud sandboxes and, since October 2026, an iOS app, for Claude Code, Codex, Cursor and OpenCode. Pro adds cloud workspaces that keep running after the app closes, multiplayer collaboration for up to five Pro users and a beta HTTP API; pricing starts at $0 locally and $50/month for Pro. Its install docs say it is not available for Windows or Linux yet, and there is no public repository. Full comparison in Conductor vs CodeAgentSwarm.

### Claude Squad [...] No. Terragon shut down. terragonlabs.com serves a page titled Terragon Shutdown, and its repository terragon-labs/terragon-oss describes the product in the past tense as a remote background agent orchestrator that ran Claude Code, Codex and other coding CLIs in the cloud. It still appears in older lists of this category, but it is no longer a choice.

No. Every tool in this guide runs on top of the coding CLIs and the subscriptions you already have. They launch Claude Code, Codex CLI, OpenCode and others as real processes, and add parallelism, isolation, diff review, notifications and session management around them. None of them is a model provider, so you still need your own account with Anthropic, OpenAI or whichever provider your agent uses.

Your agent workspace [...] ## The short answer: pick by scenario

For a desktop workspace on Windows or Linux that combines Claude Code and Codex, CodeAgentSwarm is one option: it supports ten coding agents, session status, notifications, searchable history and diff review. It is closed source and free with Pro during the open beta; provider usage is separate. This guide is published by its creator. Compare the alternatives below against your platform, licence and workflow needs.

There is no single winner here, and any list that gives you one is selling something. What you should pick depends on which constraint matters most to you: licence, platform, where you want to be sitting when you review the work, and how many agents you realistically run at once.

results.title: What It Costs to Run Claude Code or Codex in a Cloud Sandbox
results.content:
Run it in a cloud sandbox when the agent works unattended, runs in parallel or touches a repository you do not trust, and in a local container for everyday work at your desk. Anthropic’s preconfigured dev container blocks unapproved network traffic, which makes it a reasonable local home for skip-permissions runs. In the cloud, a Fly.io Sprite runs the same session for about $0.06 an hour and keeps working after the laptop closes.

### What is the best sandbox for Codex? [...] Codex sandboxes the same way locally: by default it edits and runs commands inside the project and asks before reaching further.(#src-13) Its cloud mode gives each task a workspace that keeps working while your computer sleeps.(#src-15)

A local sandbox costs nothing extra and ties the agent to the machine. The cloud earns its cents per session when the laptop has to close, when five agents would fight over one machine’s cores, or when the repository is untrusted, where Anthropic’s guidance is a dedicated VM.(#src-12)

## Claude Code Sandbox Cost on Fly.io [...] ### What is the best sandbox for Codex?

A Fly.io Sprite, for the same reason as Claude Code: Codex spends most of a session waiting on the model, and a Sprite bills only the CPU and memory actually used. Codex comes installed on new Sprites. Its own full-access mode, which drops filesystem and network restrictions, is meant for isolated environments, and a Sprite is one.

This is worth building if running agents is part of your product. For the simplest version, a rented VM with tmux, our guide to running Claude Code and Codex off your laptop walks through the setup with timings.

## Running agents in Replicas

Replicas runs each task in its own cloud VM, with your repositories cloned and the agent you choose signed in. Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and the other supported agents run there with permission prompts off. The VM doesn't have your laptop's files or logins, only the repositories and the variables you add to the environment. You can start a task from the dashboard, Slack, Linear, a GitHub or GitLab comment, the CLI or the API, and the agent opens a pull or merge request when it's done.

| How it works | [...] ## Which option to use

| If you | Use |
 --- |
| Are watching the session and want fewer prompts | Claude Code's `/sandbox` or Codex's `workspace-write` |
| Want prompts off on your own machine | Docker Sandboxes, or a container with a firewall and no host credentials mounted |
| Are building agents into your own product | A cloud sandbox |
| Want prompts off, several tasks at once, and a PR at the end | Replicas, or another of the cloud coding agents |

## Sources

Flags and behavior on this page come from each vendor's docs as of October 2026: [...] Plain containers don't restrict the network, and they share the host's kernel. Anthropic's reference devcontainer adds a firewall script that blocks outbound traffic except to GitHub, npm, the Anthropic API and a few other domains.

Docker Sandboxes is Docker's own product for running agents. `sbx run claude` starts the agent in a microVM with its own kernel, and a proxy on the host adds API keys to requests so the keys never enter the VM. It's free to run locally, supports Claude Code, Codex, OpenCode and more, and runs on macOS with Apple silicon, Windows 11 and Ubuntu 24.04 or later.

Containers and Docker Sandboxes run on your own machine, so the number of tasks you can run at once depends on its CPU and memory, and tasks stop when it sleeps.
